title: India Won't Sign the US Trade Deal Until It Gets a Better Rate Than Pakistan. That's Not Happening Anytime Soon.
excerpt: After the Supreme Court struck down Trump's sweeping tariffs, the 18% deal that looked generous in February now looks like a bad bargain. Commerce Minister Goyal says the agreement is frozen until Washington fixes the math.
body:
The India-US bilateral trade agreement that both governments spent months calling imminent is quietly going nowhere.

Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, speaking at the India Global Forum's UK-India Week in London on Saturday, said the framework agreement has been finalised but India will not implement it. The reason: India no longer has the tariff advantage over its competitors that made the deal attractive in the first place.

"We cannot implement the FTA until we secure a competitive advantage," Goyal said. "The issue currently pending is that our duties need to be lower compared to those of competing nations; once this is settled, the trade agreement will be implemented."

The problem traces back to February 6, when New Delhi agreed to lower tariffs on industrial goods and agricultural products in exchange for an 18 percent US tariff on Indian goods — well below the rates applied to Vietnam, Bangladesh, and other Asian exporters, who were facing an additional 50 percent levy under Trump's International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

That arithmetic collapsed when the US Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs, eliminating the extra levies that had made India's 18 percent rate look like a bargain. With competitors now reverting to normal Most Favoured Nation rates, the gap India was banking on has vanished.

## The Pakistan Red Line

The sticking point has sharpened into something unusually specific. Mukesh Aghi, president of the US-India Strategic Partnership Forum, confirmed the political red line at a recent summit: until Washington sets India's tariff rate at or below Pakistan's, New Delhi's negotiators will not close.

Goyal himself underscored the point at his London press conference. "The whole deal was centred around that competitive advantage we got with that 18 per cent over our neighbours and competing countries," he said. "We were lower than all our neighbouring countries and all our ASEAN countries other than Singapore. That is why the deal was attractive for us."

US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, speaking from the White House last week, insisted the deal is "99 percent there" and that only a "handful of issues" remain. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer spent two days in New Delhi last week for negotiations that both sides described as productive.

But a senior Indian government official, speaking to The Hindu Business Line on condition of anonymity, painted a bleaker picture. "There is less appetite now for tariff concessions that could spike imports without delivering equivalent export gains," the official said.

## The Ground Has Shifted

The calculus has changed on multiple fronts. India's trade surplus with the United States has narrowed. The balance of payments is under pressure from a widening trade deficit and volatile capital flows. Farmers' organisations are opposing agricultural concessions. And the USTR's ongoing Section 301 probe into alleged overcapacity and forced labour in India continues to hang over negotiations.

According to an analysis by Ajay Srivastava of the Global Trade Research Initiative, India faces lower risks if the deal falls through entirely. Once Section 122 global tariffs expire, most US imports will revert to normal MFN rates. While Section 232 tariffs on steel and aluminium will persist and new Section 301 tariffs remain possible, those proceedings are still underway.

"There is not enough reason to pre-empt those final determinations by rushing into an unfavourable deal," the official said.

Meanwhile, India has been busy elsewhere. Goyal noted that nine free trade agreements have been concluded under Prime Minister Modi's tenure with 38 countries. The India-UK FTA takes effect on July 15. An India-EU pact was signed earlier this year.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans and the hundreds of thousands of Indians on work visas in the United States, the trade deal's trajectory matters beyond tariff schedules. Bilateral trade agreements often carry provisions that affect professional services, business visas, and regulatory recognition.

A stalled deal also signals broader friction in a relationship that Indian Americans navigate daily. The diplomatic temperature between Washington and New Delhi — shaped by the Pannun affair, the visa crackdown, and now trade — affects everything from consular services to the political standing of the diaspora.

The deal is not dead. But the deal India agreed to in February no longer exists. And the one that might replace it has no timeline.

*Sources: The Hindu Business Line, The Indian Eye, Reuters, IANS*
